Spill Sink · 피라미드 연구 · Phase 5

The sharp pyramid, standalone

Phases 2–4 built tubes and put shaped floors under them. After the winding correction, the shape that had been playing the floor — a plain field of sharp pyramids, nothing in front of it — leads every axis this study scores. Phase 5 is the focused case for and against building exactly that.

All three axes, oriented geometry

designtotal worst-ρ ↓smear ↑ (beam width 2 mm) head-on ↓
sharp pyramid p5.5 / d500.134 %4.160.0271
sharp pyramid p2 / d18 (Phase 5.4)0.130 %4.100.0272
truncated pyramid0.172 %4.510.2010
blade + pyramid stack0.184 %3.950.0851
cone0.215 %4.060.0595

Total: worst over 5 angles × 3 coating models (sweep_rewind.csv). Smear and head-on: published form protocol, 16 stripe phases × 512 spp (form_pyr.json). The pyramid leads all three; a single press-formed layer beats the two-layer blade assembly — the previous champion — on every number, including a 3.1× advantage on head-on brightness. Caveat added in Phase 5.8: every number in this table is at azimuth 0, and the total-axis lead does not survive the worst azimuth — see “The azimuth hole” below.

Why the front layers lost

The study’s one repeated law is that flat area facing the viewer at the mouth decides the ranking — tip radius, apex flats, blade edges and honeycomb wall-tops are all the same variable. A tube in front of the pyramid can only add such area (blade edges, wall tops) while blocking the surface that was already best. The honeycomb, second on total reflectance in Phase 2, ends Phase 5 with no role: its wall tops face the viewer like the flat plate it was meant to replace, and the floor that fixed its normal-incidence number outperforms it standing alone.

The periodicity objection, measured and dismissed

The pyramid field is periodic, and this project bans periodic arrays because a scanning beam over identical cells returns a repeating glint. That objection was measured here rather than assumed: the form protocol walks the stripe across one full pitch and records the spread of the head-on peak (peak_ratio_span).

varianttotal worst-ρ ↓smear ↑ (beam width 2 mm) head-on ↓vs periodic span θ0 / ±40°
periodic (no jitter)0.134 %4.160.0271+0.0 %1.01× / 1.4×
apex jitter 0.30.140 %——+4.5 %—
apex jitter 0.60.156 %——+16.8 %—
apex jitter 0.6 + tip drop 0.150.166 %3.280.0270+24.2 %1.03× / 1.9×

An em-dash means that axis was not run for that variant; the form protocol was run on the two ends of the jitter series and they agree to three decimals on both axes.

The periodic pyramid’s phase spread is 1.01× at normal incidence — the 1D groove that motivated the rule measured 214×. A cell that closes in both directions is phase-uniform on its own, so the de-periodising jitter buys nothing and costs up to a quarter of the total-reflectance budget. Build it periodic: one die, no jitter schedule.

Prediction scoreboard, Phase 5.1

Held — the un-jittered anchor reproduced sweep_rewind exactly; mean smear/head-on unmoved by jitter.
Wrong — “apex jitter is nearly free (≤10 %)”: it costs +16.8 % at 0.6 and +24.2 % with tip drop.
Wrong — “the span collapses under jitter”: there was nothing to collapse. The premise of the no-periodic-array rule does not apply to doubly-closed cells.

Mixed sizes, the RF-chamber look (Phase 5.3)

fieldtotal worst-ρ ↓smear ↑ (beam width 2 mm) head-on ↓vs uniform small
uniform small (anchor)0.134 %4.160.0271—
mixed, equal depth0.171 %——+28 %
mixed, equal slope0.188 %——+40 %

The mixed fields were rejected on the total axis alone (28–40 % behind before the other axes could matter), so their form protocol was not run.

RF mixes sizes for broadband absorption — each pyramid works at wavelengths near its own size. That is a wave mechanism with no ray-optics analogue, and the measurement agrees: the mix lands between its parts on the aspect curve, 28–40 % behind tiling the panel with the small pitch alone. The chamber photograph is not a trick worth copying here; it solves a problem this wall does not have.

The buildable pyramid (Phase 5.4)

The champion cell is a 9:1 needle — base 5.5 mm, height 50 mm — and no die can press it, no press can hold its mathematically sharp apex. Two escapes were pre-registered and measured together: scale (only the ratio depth/pitch matters to ray optics, so grow the cell) and tip tolerance (only the ratio tip/pitch should matter, so a bigger cell also buys a blunter allowed tip).

designtip / pitchflat frac total worst-ρ ↓smear ↑ (beam width 2 mm) head-on ↓
champion p5.5 / d50 (anchor)0.0 / 60.00 %0.134 %4.160.0271
p10 / d90, sharp0.0 / 100.00 %0.143 %1.270.0270
p10 / d90, tip 0.5 (build spec)0.5 / 100.25 %0.143 %3.230.0432
p10 / d90, tip 1.01.0 / 101.00 %0.148 %3.270.0740
p10 / d90, tip 2.02.0 / 104.00 %0.176 %2.650.1485
p2 / d18, sharp (thin option)0.0 / 20.00 %0.130 %4.100.0272
p2 / d18, tip 0.10.1 / 20.25 %0.130 %4.480.0590

Three laws separated here. Total reflectance follows aspect alone — all three scales sit within a few percent. Form destruction does not scale: the probe stripe is a fixed 2 mm, and a 10 mm cell carries it on one flank nearly unbroken (smear 1.27 against the champion’s 4.16), so the cell must stay no coarser than the beam it is meant to shred. And the tip flat taxes the head-on axis, worse at coarse pitch where it also revives the scanning glint the periodic rule worries about (phase span 12.9× at tip 2.0 versus 1.02× sharp). The three-axis winner is the thin field — pitch 2, depth 18, panel 20 mm with backing, 0.130 % total — IF its sub-0.1 mm tips can be formed; the 0.1 mm-tip row above prices the failure to hold that (head-on 0.0590, 2.2× sharp). The coarse field p10/d90 with tip 0.5 stays the fallback where fine tooling is unavailable: same total, but a third of the smear and a 4.3× phase span.

The probe beam was an assumption (Phase 5.5)

Every smear and span number above is conditioned on a 2 mm probe stripe — a protocol constant, not a measurement. The user’s projector (LaserCube Ultra MK2: 4 mm aperture, 1 mrad divergence) puts roughly a 7–14 mm beam on the wall at 3–10 m. So the stripe width became a swept variable, and a first-class input in the simulator.

pitchbeamsmear ↑ (beam width 2 mm)head-on ↓ span θ0return width / flat’s, mm @−40°
2 (d18)2 (protocol)4.100.02721.01×3.23 / 0.78
5 mm1.790.02731.00×3.41 / 1.90
10 mm1.040.02731.00×3.93 / 3.77
5.5 (d50)2 (protocol)4.160.02711.01×3.15 / 0.78
5 mm1.820.02731.01×3.36 / 1.90
10 mm1.080.02731.00×3.97 / 3.77
10 (d90)2 (protocol)1.270.02701.02×1.07 / 0.78
5 mm0.790.02721.01×1.59 / 1.90
10 mm0.650.02741.01×2.56 / 3.77

The ratio metric compresses as the beam widens because the FLAT control blurs too: the fine-pitch panels return a ∼3–4 mm smudge whose width the panel itself sets (3.93 mm at beam 10 against the flat wall’s 3.77), while pitch 10 returns a stripe NARROWER than the flat wall’s at every beam width (smear 0.65 at beam 10) — its flanks act as mirrors that keep the stripe a stripe. A wider real beam therefore does NOT rehabilitate the coarse pitch; the fine-pitch fields stay at or above the flat wall’s blur at one ninth of its brightness, and the form axis simply loses discriminating power as the beam itself arrives pre-blurred. Head-on and total never see the beam; the three-axis verdict of Phase 5.4 stands at every width measured.

The coating parameter nobody measured (Phase 5.6)

Every number in this report was taken at spec_roughness = 0.30 — a pinned value that has never been measured on the physical paint. The winner and the flat-plate denominator were re-measured across 0.10–0.50, all three axes where it matters.

roughnessp2/d18 total ↓flat total advantagep2 smear ↑p2 head-on ↓
0.100.099 %1.141 %11.6×4.160.0089
0.200.103 %1.141 %11.0×——

0.400.231 %1.142 %4.9×——
0.500.384 %1.141 %3.0×4.050.0665

The flat plate is roughness-invariant (ρdh integrates the hemisphere; the lobe only moves within it) and sits exactly on the historical 1.1413 % — but the winner swings 3.9× across the same range: rough paint diffuses the first bounce back out of the cavity instead of chaining it down. Every “N× darker than flat” claim is conditional on the paint’s unmeasured lobe width: N runs from 3.0× to 11.6×. The design choice survives everywhere; the single number does not. Measuring one painted coupon is now worth more than any further simulation. The 0.30 row is the value the rest of this report is quoted at. (Self-test: pure-diffuse rows at 0.10 and 0.50 read 0.130 % / 0.130 % — identical, so the harness does not leak roughness into the diffuse shader. A measurement-frame defect found during this sweep — a margin-less flat reads 21 % low at face 60 — is documented in FINDINGS_phase56_roughness.md; the first run's flat rows were superseded before publication.)

The die tolerance, settled (Phase 5.8, part 1)

Between “mathematically sharp” and the 0.1 mm tip that already measured a 2.2× head-on penalty, nothing was measured — so the drawing could not carry a tolerance. The pre-registered rule: the tolerance is the largest tip whose head-on stays ≤1.5× sharp.

tip, mm (pitch 2)flat fracsmear ↑ (beam width 2 mm) head-on ↓span θ0
0.000.00 %4.100.02721.01×
0.020.01 %4.160.02821.06×
0.050.06 %4.270.03441.35×
0.100.25 %4.480.05902.20×
0.150.56 %4.710.09632.20×

Head-on is linear in the flat fraction at fixed pitch, and at fixed fraction a finer pitch pays more (p5.5 with a 0.275 mm tip, same 0.25 % fraction, reads 0.0552). By the 1.5× rule the winner’s drawing carries tip flat ≤ 0.05 mm (0.0344 passes, the 0.1 mm tip’s 0.0590 fails); the same rule interpolates to ∼0.19 mm at pitch 5.5 and ∼0.46 mm at pitch 10 — tolerance is bought with pitch, and only the head-on axis charges for it.

The azimuth hole (Phase 5.8, part 2)

Every pyramid total in this report was measured at azimuth 0 — and the brief says the beam azimuth is unknown. Rotating the panel about its own normal (the control pinned at 0.0500 in every row):

azimuth φworst-ρ (p2/d18)vs φ0
0°0.130 %+0 %
05°0.142 %+9 %
10°0.184 %+42 %
15°0.206 %+58 %
20°0.217 %+67 %
22.5°0.217 %+66 %
25°0.216 %+66 %
30°0.226 %+74 %
35°0.225 %+73 %
40°0.198 %+53 %
45°0.196 %+51 %

The worst azimuth is a broad plateau near 30° at 0.226 % — +74 % over the published φ-0 number, scale-invariant (the champion reads 0.193 % at φ45), and only half-fixed by √2 more depth (0.174 % at φ45 for p2/d25.5). On worst-over-azimuth totals the pyramid (0.226 %) loses narrowly to the rotationally symmetric cone (0.215 %, φ-invariant by symmetry). The pyramid keeps a 2.2× head-on lead measured at φ0; whether it survives φ30 is unmeasured and is the next experiment, together with a thin cone field at matched aspect.

Prediction scoreboard, Phase 5.8

Held — head-on linear in flat fraction; cross-pitch ordering held; the 0.05 mm spec rule confirmed as pre-registered
Wrong — “the pyramid is azimuth-safe (≤6 %)”: it is not — +74 % at φ30, the largest single miss of Phase 5, and the reason the total-axis crown is now shared with the cone
Wrong — “the worst azimuth is the diagonal and √2 depth fixes it”: the worst is φ≈30° and the fix recovers only half

The deciding round: pyramid vs cone at the worst azimuth (Phase 5.9)

The azimuth hole put the cone back in the race. This round measured the pyramid’s form axes at φ30 (the form protocol gained an azimuth input, guarded by an exact φ0 re-run), re-anchored the cone, and asked whether the cone can be thin.

pyramid p2/d18thin cone p2/d18.2 verdict (>8 % rule)
total, worst-φ0.226 % (φ30)0.215 % (φ-invariant)tie (5.3 % apart)
smear, worst-φ ↑2.44 (φ30; 4.10 at φ0)2.77cone, by 14 %
head-on ↓0.0272 (identical at φ0/φ30)0.0464pyramid, by 41 %
panel incl. backing20 mm20.2 mmtie

The pre-registered rule ends 1:1:1 with the thickness tiebreak indiscriminate — a genuine draw — and is broken by Phase 5.5: the cone’s smear edge is protocol-conditioned (at the real 7–14 mm beam every design’s smear ratio compresses toward 1), while the pyramid’s head-on edge is beam-independent AND now azimuth-independent. One edge survives deployment; the other does not. The pyramid keeps the crown — p2/d18, tip ≤0.05 mm, 20 mm panel — with its worst-azimuth total honestly stated as cone-equal (0.226 % vs 0.215 %), and the thin cone stands as a fully valid alternate: azimuth-immune by construction, same panel, same total, 1.7× brighter head-on. The big cone’s anchor re-measured at 0.215 % against the rewind value 0.2160 % — and the thin cone proves the cone family scale-invariant too.

Wrong — smear at phi 30 predicted 2.6–3.8, measured 2.44; thin-cone smear predicted 4.0 ± 0.6, measured 2.77 — shrinking any family against the fixed 2 mm stripe cuts its smear

The cone’s head-on penalty is its TIP CAP, not the interstices between bases: shrinking the tip radius from 0.073 to 0.03 mm took head-on from 0.0464 to 0.0317, landing in the pre-registered tip-area band. The gap to the pyramid narrowed from 1.7× to 1.17× — and this cone needs no azimuth caveat at all, with the best worst-over-φ total on the board (0.212 %). The choice between the two finalists is now a tooling question (≤0.05 mm square tip vs ≤0.03 mm tip radius), not an optical one. Separately, the pyramid’s aspect law holds to pitch 1: an 11 mm panel reads 0.130 % at φ0, priced at a ~0.022 mm tip tolerance.

Closing audit: the verdict’s single-point legs (Phase 5.11)

Held — the thin cone's azimuth immunity and seed robustness are measurements now, not assertions: 0.207 %–0.217 % across φ 0/22.5/45 and three seeds (4.5 % spread)
Held — the drawing spec and the azimuth hole do not compound: pyramid tip 0.05 at φ30 reads 0.225 % total, head-on 0.0286, span 1.01× — every number inside its pre-registered band. Six predictions, six held; Phase 5's design questions are closed. What remains is physical: one painted coupon, one beam-spot measurement, two tooling quotes.

The pre-coupon worst envelope (Phase 5.12)

The deployed panel faces two unknowns at once — paint lobe width and beam azimuth. The joint worst, per finalist:

r 0.10r 0.30r 0.50
pyramid p2/d18, worst-φ0.226 %0.226 %0.385 %
cone p2/d18.2 r0.03 (φ-invariant)0.212 %0.212 %0.390 %
flat plate (roughness-invariant)1.141 % at every roughness

Smooth paint buys nothing on totals — the roughness-invariant pure-diffuse envelope owns both floors (its payoff is head-on: 0.0089 vs 0.0665 across the range, Phase 5.6). Rough paint costs both finalists nearly equally, and at the joint worst they read 0.385 % vs 0.390 % — 1.4 % apart, within noise. The pre-coupon claim for either design: 3× to 5× darker than a flat Musou wall; one painted coupon collapses that range to a number. The measurement campaign ends here — every remaining question needs an object, not a render.

The easy-build tier (Phase 5.15)

Can a LOW pyramid be rescued by a bought honeycomb in front? The stack is measurably azimuth-flat — the one thing the pyramid is not — but the top layer owns the axes that survive deployment:

designtotal φ0total φ30 smear ↑ (beam width 2 mm)head-on ↓tip req. panel
easy pyramid p4/d20 (aspect 5)0.179 %0.251 %4.090.0272~0.2 mm22 mm
bought comb 35 mm + pyramid floor 15 mm0.225 %0.225 %0.970.0979off-the-shelf52 mm

The stack does win one axis — its total does not move with azimuth at all (0.0 % shift, the hex walls) — but the comb’s wall tops own head-on (0.0979, 3.6× the pyramid’s) and its smear is a flat wall’s. The better easy option is the half-steep pyramid itself: single pressed part, tip tolerance 4× looser than the p2 spec, head-on identical to the finalists, and only 11–19 % behind them on worst-φ totals. Its azimuth hole is also relatively milder (+41 % vs the aspect-9 field’s +74 %). Floor depth under a comb was confirmed irrelevant (15 mm floor reads like Phase 4’s 3–5 mm floors) — the top layer owns the result.

The coarse tier (pitch ≥ 10, big honeycomb and its combinations) is a separate report: Phase 6.

The ordering package (Phase 5.13)

Four STLs now exist in export/, built by the same build_mesh calls every sweep ran, round-trip-verified and kernel-clean: the two spec parts (for mould/CNC quotes) and two 2×-scale print coupons whose tips a resin printer can approach. The 2× pyramid coupon’s targets are pre-registered:

As-built envelopes differ from the nominal face — the builder skirts one pitch of rim per side (pyramid coupons 68×68 and 76×76 mm) and jittered cones overhang by a base radius; quotes must carry the manifest dimensions (export/finalists_manifest.json), not 60×60. One prediction missed in the good direction: the 2× coupon smears 4.53, not the 1.2–2.2 a beam/pitch model predicted — the coarse-pitch smear cliff sits between pitch 5.5 and 10, not at a fixed beam ratio. Grading: P1–P3 held (round trip ×4, kernel-clean ×4, all three coupon axes), P4 wrong as stated. The rim was verified harmless by inspection — one extra ring of full-depth cells, 3.6 mm² of flat on a 5776 mm² part — so the lab and the simulation measure the same texture and the acceptance bands stand for both coupons.

Validity check: none of this is a face-size artifact (Phase 5.7)

Every total in this phase was measured on a 60 mm coupon. After a measurement-frame defect surfaced on flat slabs at that size, the champion and the winner were re-measured at 100 mm:

designface 60face 100shift
champion p5.5 / d500.134 %0.130 %-2.7 %
winner p2 / d180.130 %0.130 %-0.1 %

Both inside the pre-registered ±4–5 % bands: the phase’s numbers are properties of the designs, not of the coupon size. The flat-slab defect is confined to margin-less slabs and flat references are now measured at face 100 (they reproduce the closed-form curve there: 1.030 % worst against the model’s 1.030 %). The one anomaly 5.6 left open is closed: a “fully truncated” pyramid field was never flat — the builder clamps the tip at 0.8×pitch, and the residual 0.4 mm grooves absorb a genuine third of the return (FINDINGS_phase57_faceinvariance.md).

What Phase 5 still owes

A physical coupon remains the only test of the coating model. And every number here is one seed; the periodic conclusion should survive seeds trivially, but the claim has not been bought yet.

Corrections that led here are logged in the errata page; the winding defect and its re-measurement are FINDINGS_winding.md and FINDINGS_formpyr.md.
